## About xdssat

### What is xdssat?

A bridge between the DSSAT crop model and Python. It writes the DSSAT engine's own input files (experiment,
weather, soil and cultivar files) for every grid cell and season of a region, runs the engine many times in
parallel, and collects the results into one netCDF file that xarray can read. [What xdssat is](xdssat/index.qmd)
explains the idea; [How xdssat differs from common DSSAT use](xdssat/gridding.qmd) compares it with running
DSSAT one field at a time.

### Is xdssat part of DSSAT?

No. xdssat is an independent project, not developed, endorsed or supported by the DSSAT Foundation. It uses the
DSSAT engine as it is published. See [Acknowledgements and how to cite](acknowledgements.qmd).

### Does xdssat change the crop models?

No. It does not reimplement or patch the models: every simulated number comes from the unmodified DSSAT-CSM
engine (`dscsm048`). xdssat only prepares the engine's inputs and reads its outputs.

### Which version of DSSAT does it use?

DSSAT-CSM 4.8. The engine on this site was built from version 4.8.6.4 of the
[published source code](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os).

### Do I need DSSAT installed?

You need the engine, in one of two ways: build it from source with `scripts/build_engine.py` (needs gfortran,
cmake and make), or point xdssat at an existing DSSAT 4.8 installation on Windows. Both routes are in
[Getting started](getting-started.md), section 2.

### Which crops can it simulate?

The DSSAT engine covers many crops (48 crop codes in the files listed on the
[training page](learn/index.qmd)). xdssat builds every experiment file from a template experiment, and the
repository currently ships one template, for rice (`templates/XDRI8601.RIX`). Another crop needs its own template
experiment; that has not been tested yet.

### Which regions can it run?

The weather and soil caches are built for all of Indonesia, on the 0.1° grid of AgERA5. One area of interest is
defined so far, Java (`--aoi java`), because the irrigation classes it uses exist only for Java. Adding another
region means adding its box and region name in the code and an irrigation map for it.

### Where do the weather and soil data come from?

Weather: daily AgERA5 reanalysis from the Copernicus Climate Change Service, at 0.1°. Soil: SoilGrids 2.0
texture and organic carbon at six depths, turned into DSSAT soil profiles with the Saxton and Rawls equations.
Everything is listed on the [case study's Data page](java/data.qmd).

### How long does a run take?

The current case-study run simulated ${fmt.int(cur.seasons)} seasons (${fmt.int(cur.strata)} strata in
${fmt.int(cur.cells)} cells of Java, 1991-2020) in ${fmt.d1(cur.minutes)} minutes, with ${cur.workers} engine
processes in parallel. A quick test on 30 cells and 2 years takes about 20 seconds
([Getting started](getting-started.md), section 7). Preparing the inputs once takes longer: about 1.5 hours
in total, mostly downloading and caching weather and soil data (section 6).

### What does a run produce?

One netCDF file per run, on the 0.1° grid, with yield, biomass, season length, water and nitrogen variables and
the key dates for each water regime, season and cell. Its full structure is on
[How xdssat differs from common DSSAT use](xdssat/gridding.qmd).

## About the case study

### Why do the simulated yields differ from the official statistics?

A crop model simulates the yield its inputs allow: the weather, the soil, the cultivar and the management written
into the experiment file. Official statistics reflect everything else that happens on real farms as well. The
case study compares the two district by district and calibrates a soil fertility factor against the
statistics. The [Scientific method](java/science.qmd) page shows how close they get and what remains.

### Does the website run DSSAT in my browser?

No. The engine runs on the author's machine; the pages read small CSV and JSON files exported from its results
and draw the charts in the browser. The [Rebuild notes](rebuild.qmd) show how those files are made.

## About the training

### Is this the official DSSAT training?

No. The [DSSAT training](learn/index.qmd) section is adapted from the 2018 DSSAT training in Chiang Mai,
Thailand, and follows its syllabus and exercises, but it is written for this site. The course's slides and
exercise sheets are not reproduced. For official training, see the [DSSAT website](https://dssat.net).

### Do I need xdssat to follow the training?

To read the pages, no: every chart is already computed. To run the [notebooks](notebooks/index.qmd) yourself,
yes: they use xdssat's Python code to write the files and run the engine, plus the DSSAT example data
(`dssat-csm-data`) next to this repository. The
[training overview](learn/index.qmd#what-you-need-to-run-the-notebooks) lists what they need.

### Why do some modules end with a map of Java?

Modules 1, 2, 3 and 5 close with a section called "From one field to a grid: xdssat". It takes the module's
single-field idea (phenology, weather, soil water, yield risk) and shows it for every cell of the case study.
That is the step xdssat adds to what the course teaches.

## Using and citing

### How do I cite xdssat and DSSAT?

Cite DSSAT as the DSSAT Foundation asks, and xdssat with the version you used. The exact references are on
[Acknowledgements and how to cite](acknowledgements.qmd).

### What is the licence?

xdssat is released under the
[Mozilla Public License 2.0](https://github.com/bennyistanto/xdssat/blob/main/LICENSE). DSSAT and the data sets
keep their own terms.

### Where do I report a problem or ask a question?

In the [xdssat issue tracker](https://github.com/bennyistanto/xdssat/issues). Every page also has a "Report an
issue" link. Questions about the DSSAT engine itself belong with the [DSSAT team](https://dssat.net), but please
do not send them problems that come from xdssat.
